prize_parts.citation: For the development of targeted protein degradation, in which small molecules are designed to direct the ubiquitin-proteasome system to chosen proteins and remove them

statement.case_for: I keep targeted protein degradation as my single preferred part. The achievement is a design principle: a small molecule is built to bring a chosen protein and an E3 ligase together, so recognition chemistry becomes event-driven removal instead of occupancy-driven inhibition. This makes targets addressable that binding-site pharmacology could not reach. The concept (Crews and Deshaies, 2001) is original, and Ciulli's structure-guided VHL ligands and ternary-complex work turned it into rational, reproducible, drug-like chemistry used well beyond the original groups. The chair's summary shows it has the widest base in this committee, and the reasons given are scientific, not a head count: independent reproduction, a clear mechanism, and a measurable change in what chemists, biologists and clinicians can do. Round 1 did not weaken my view; it clarified what the citation must say.
statement.case_against: Two reservations remain and I do not dismiss them. First, no approved heterobifunctional degrader is cited, so clinical validation is incomplete and the field leans on few E3 ligases (CRBN, VHL). I still do not think this should decide a chemistry prize, which rewards the new capability and the chemical principle, but I accept it makes the citation wording important. Second, attribution: the molecular-glue lineage (Handa and Ito on cereblon; Sakamoto, Kim, Gray and others) has serious claims that a three-name credit leaves out. Any trio is an exclusion, and the citation should say plainly that it recognizes the design of bifunctional degraders and does not claim to settle the glue story. I also remain unsure how much of degrader chemistry is new beyond linker and ligand optimization around an existing cellular mechanism, although I judge the principle itself to be new.

responses.point: Chabes would credit Handa in place of Ciulli and phrase the citation around the glue branch as well, so the glue and PROTAC strands are both represented.
responses.response: Your question about what the citation actually covers is the right one, and I have reconsidered the swap. I still keep Ciulli. Handa identified cereblon as the thalidomide target, which is a decisive mechanistic result, but it is target identification for an existing drug. The chemistry we would be honouring is the deliberate design of molecules that recruit an E3 ligase, and Ciulli's VHL ligands and ternary-complex structures are what made that design rational. I do not want to hide the glue lineage, so my citation is worded around directing the ubiquitin-proteasome system to chosen proteins and my case_against states openly that glue contributors are excluded. If the committee finds that Handa's cereblon work belongs in the credit, that is a debate about whether this is one achievement or two, and I would sooner have it openly than swap a name quietly.

responses.point: Sparr ranks degraders only eighth and prefers phase separation, with lipid nanoparticles second, citing maturity and attribution.
responses.response: I read your round-1 B049 case carefully, and I agree on the physical-chemical clarity of condensate work. I also appreciate that you named your own field bias. But the critique you accept, that many reported cellular condensates may be overexpression or in vitro artefacts, bears directly on what a citation can claim today, whereas for degraders the molecular event (ubiquitination and loss of a named protein) is directly measured and independently reproduced. On attribution I accept your point that three names are a cut, but B049 has the same problem with Pappu, Mittag and Rosen, so it does not favour B049. I would still welcome an answer to the chair's question on whether maturity alone is what keeps degraders at the bottom of your ranking.

responses.point: Linke, the chair, ranked phase separation first at opening but now prefers degraders, and notes that the cellular phase-separation evidence is contested.
responses.response: I agree with your round-1 judgement that degraders have an unambiguous chemical output and that B049 should wait for firmer evidence on in-cell function. I also note that your move from first place for B049 to B067 is a stated scientific reassessment, and I do not treat it as a confirmation of my own position; our agreement on Ciulli rests on the same reading of the chemistry, not on independent evidence. Where I would press you is on the chair's own question: if the committee does choose to broaden the citation to cover the glue branch, would you still hold to three names, and which would you drop?

responses.point: Somfai prefers Pd-catalyzed C-N coupling as the mature, clean-credit method and lists degraders only as first alternative.
responses.response: Your point that C-N coupling is the best verified case for maturity and clean two-person credit is fair, and I have no quarrel with its quality. My difficulty is the 2010 prize: the citation would have to show a distinct bond-forming achievement and, as you note, Kosugi leaves a precedence footnote, so the novelty margin is thin. Degraders open a new class of targets and a design approach, which I weigh above refinement of a method that is already routine. I would ask what specific evidence on degraders, such as an approval or a late-stage readout, would be needed for you to move it from first alternative to your preferred part.

uncertainties: Whether the committee judges PROTACs and molecular glues to be one achievement or two, which decides if Handa or Ciulli is the third name
Whether clinical validation is sufficient in 2026 without an approved degrader
How strongly priority claims for the cereblon and glue strands should weigh against the PROTAC design lineage
My credit assessment rests on recalled history, not independent verification
statement.conflict_note: No change to my earlier disclosure. I have no direct link to any shortlisted candidate. My postdoc mentors (Molly Stevens, Freddy Boey) and the Linkoping sensor tradition are unconnected to any shortlisted discovery. I overlap scientifically with Emma Sparr on peptide and lipid self-assembly, relevant to B049 and B047, but this is not a recusal matter.
